(مكية [إلا آية 87 فمدنية] وهي تسع وتسعون آية [نزلت بعد سورة يوسف] ) بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

(Meccan [except verse 87, which is Medinan], and it has ninety-nine verses [it was revealed after Surah Yusuf]) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿تِلْكَ﴾ ("These") refers to the verses contained in the surah (chapter). ﴿الكتاب﴾ ("the Book") and ﴿القرآن المبين﴾ ("the clear Qur'an") refer to the surah.

The indefiniteness of ﴿قرآن﴾ ("Qur'an") is for magnification. The meaning: these are the verses of the Book, which is perfect in being a Book, and what a clear Qur'an it is. It is as if it were said: the Book that combines perfection and wondrous clarity of exposition.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verses 2–3:

It is recited as rubbama and rubbamata with shaddah (doubled ba'), and as rubbama and rubama with damma and fatha with lightening (takhfif). If you ask: why has it (rubama) entered upon the present tense (muda'ari') when they (the grammarians) have refused its entry except upon the past tense (madi)? I say: because what is awaited (al-mutarraqqab) in God the Exalted's report is in the position of the past tense that is certain in its realization, so it is as if it were said: "Rubama wadda" (perhaps they will wish). If you ask: when will their wishing be? I say:

At death, or on the Day of Resurrection when they see their state and the state of the Muslims. It has also been said: when they see the Muslims coming out of the Fire, and this too is a kind of wishing. If you ask: then what is the meaning of the diminution (al-taqlil)? [[Mahmud said: "If you say: what is the meaning of diminishing their wishing... etc.?" Ahmad says: There is no doubt that the Arabs often express a meaning by what conveys the opposite of its intended sense, and from it is his saying:

"I may leave the Qur'an with its fingertips yellowed"

and he only praises by abundance of this, and he has expressed with qad, which conveys diminution, and from it: "and God knows best." "And indeed you know that I am the Messenger of God" (Qur'an 61:5); the intent is to rebuke them for their harming Musa, peace be upon him, despite the abundance of their knowledge of his prophethood and his sincere advice to them. The scholars of rhetoric (ulama al-bayan) have differed in explaining this. Some explained it by what al-Zamakhshari mentioned just above, namely alerting the lesser to the greater; and some explained it by saying that the intent in it is to announce that the meaning has reached its extreme limit, so that it nearly returns to its opposite, and this is the nature of everything that reaches its end, that it reverts to its reverse. Abu al-Tayyib has made this clear in his saying:

"You were so generous that you nearly sifted a sieve for the bounded and for joy, weeping."

Both of these explanations carry the speech toward exaggeration with a kind of alerting to it, and the reliance in this is upon the context of the speech, for when it requires, for example, abundance, and there enters into it an expression whose outward form suggests diminution, the hearer awakens to the understanding that the intent is exaggeration by one of the two methods mentioned, and God knows best.]] I say: it comes upon the Arabs' way in their saying: "Perhaps you will regret your action," and "a person may regret what he has done," while they have no doubt about his regret, nor do they intend to minimize it; rather they mean: if the regret were doubtful or small, it would be incumbent upon you not to do this action, because the wise guard against exposing themselves to a suspected harm, just as they guard against the certain and against its small portion as against its large. Likewise the meaning in the verse: if they were to wish for Islam even once, it would be more fitting that they hasten to it; so how (much more so) when they wish for it at every hour. "Had they been Muslims" is the report of their wishing, and it was expressed in the third-person form because they are the ones being reported about, like your saying: "He swore by God that he would certainly do it." Had it been said: "He swore by God, 'I will certainly do it, and had we been Muslims'," it would have been good and sound. It has also been said: the terrors of that day will bewilder them so that they remain stunned; then if at some moments they come to themselves from their silence, they wish, and therefore the diminution is used. "Leave them" (dharhum) means: cut off your hope of their turning back, and leave them from forbidding what they are upon and turning them away from it by reminder and counsel; "let them eat and enjoy themselves" with their worldly life (dunya) [[His saying "and enjoy themselves with their worldly life" — in al-Sihah: the world was named for its nearness (dunuw), its plural is duna, like al-kubra and al-kubar, and al-sughra and al-sughar. (Ayn)]] and the execution of their desires, and let their hope and expectation of long life and the soundness of their affairs occupy them, and that they should meet in the outcome nothing but good. "Then they will come to know" the evil of their conduct.

The purpose is to announce that they are among the people of abandonment, that nothing will come from them except what they are in, and that there is no restrainer or admonisher for them except witnessing what they are warned of, at a time when admonition will not benefit them, and there is no way for them to take heed before that. So He commanded His Messenger to leave them to themselves and not to occupy himself with what has no benefit, and to exaggerate in leaving them, until he commands them with what will only increase their regret in the end. In it is the establishment of proof, exaggeration in warning, and an excuse. In it is also an alert that preferring pleasure and luxury, and what long hope leads to, is this: this is the habit of most people and is not the character of believers. It is reported from some of them: wallowing in the world is the character of the perishing.

And to it is a Book known (the decreed term). ﴿A Book known﴾: a written Book, known. It is their term (ajal), which was written and specified on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh). He made "community" feminine at the beginning and masculine at the end, taking first the wording and then the meaning into account. And He said ﴿nor do they delay﴾, omitting "from it" (ʿanhu) because it is understood.

Al-A'mash recited: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down" (يا أيها الذي ألقى عليه الذكر). [[His words "الذي ألقى عليه الذكر" are perhaps meant to be: إليه. (ع)]] This call from them seems to be in a mocking manner, just as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾. How could they acknowledge that the Reminder was sent down to him while attributing him to madness? Inversion in their speech for mockery and derision is a broad practice. It has come in the Book of Allah in several places, among them: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾, and ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾. It is also found frequently in the speech of non-Arabs. The meaning is: "Indeed, you speak the words of madmen when you claim that Allah has sent down the Reminder upon you."

The Arabic footnote-style text in this passage is part of the commentary, so I translate it as it stands.

"Law" (لو) combined with "la" (لا) and "ma" (ما) gives two meanings: the negation of one thing because another thing exists, and the meaning of tahdid (urging). As for "hal" (هل), it is only combined with "la" alone, for the meaning of tahdid. Ibn Muqbil said:

"Law ma al-hayaa wa-law ma al-deena 'ibtukuma ... bi-ba'di ma fikuma idh 'ibtuma 'awari"

[Ibn Muqbil; and the explanation of "lawla" and "law ma": their origin is "law," which indicates the non-occurrence of one thing due to the non-occurrence of another. It was combined with the negating "la" and "ma," so together they indicate the occurrence of one thing due to the existence of another, since the negation of a negation is an affirmation. If it has no answer (jawab), then with them in the present tense it indicates tahdid, and in other tenses it indicates reproach or rebuke. He says: "Lawla al-hayaa" (if not for shame) exists, and "law ma al-deen" (if not for religion) exists; I would have criticized you both for some of what is in you both, since you both criticized me for my faults, or I would have enumerated them as a defect.]

The meaning: "Why do you not bring us the angels, who would testify to your truthfulness and support you in your warning," like His saying, ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he would be with him as a warner?﴾ Or: "Why do you not bring us the angels to punish us for our denial of you, if you are truthful, as the denying nations were visited by angels with their messengers?"

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verse 8:

It is read "tanazzalu" (meaning "tatanazzalu"), and "tunazzalu" on the passive form of "nazzala," and "nunazzilu al-malaikata" with the nun and the accusative "al-malaikata." ﴿Except with truth﴾: that is, We do not send them down except as a descent accompanied by wisdom and benefit. There is no wisdom in their coming to you visibly, so that you see them and they bear witness to you of the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), because you would then be believers out of compulsion. A similar statement is His, exalted be He, ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾. It was also said: the truth is the revelation, or the punishment. "Idhan" is both a response and a condition, because it is a response to them and a conditional answer to an implied condition, whose meaning is:

"And if We had sent down the angels, they would not have been given respite, and their punishment would not have been deferred."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verse 9:

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ rejects their denial and mockery. [[Mahmud said: "This is a rebuttal of their denial and mockery..." etc. Ahmad said: It may also be meant that it is preserved from what would disgrace it, such as contradiction and discrepancy, which are not absent from fabricated speech. This too is evidence that it is from God, as He, exalted is He, says in another verse: "Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy" (Qur'an 4:82).]] in their saying: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down" (Qur'an 15:6). Therefore He said: "Indeed, We" (innā naḥnu), emphasizing against them that He is the One who sent it down, with certainty and finality, and that it is He who sent it with Jibril to Muhammad (ﷺ), with watchers before him and behind him (Qur'an 72:27), until it descended and reached (its destination) preserved from the devils, and He is its guardian at all times, from every addition, deficiency, distortion and alteration. This is unlike the earlier scriptures, for He did not undertake to preserve them; rather, He entrusted their preservation to the rabbis (al-rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (al-aḥbar), and they differed among themselves out of envy, so distortion occurred. He did not leave the Qur'an to other than its Guardian. If you say: when His saying "Indeed, We sent down the Reminder" was a rebuttal of their denial and mockery, how is His saying "and indeed We are its guardians" connected to it? I say: He made that a proof that it was sent down from Him by a sign, for if it were the speech of a human or something other than a sign, addition and deficiency would have entered it as they enter every other speech. It was also said: the pronoun in lahu (its) refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as in His saying: "And God will protect you" (Qur'an 5:67).

in the sects of the former peoples (fi shiya' al-awwalin), that is, in their factions and groups. Al-shi'ah (sect) is a group of people when they agree upon a doctrine and a way. The meaning of "We sent him among them" is: We made him a prophet among them and made him a messenger to them. "And there did not come to them" is a narration of a past situation, because "ma" (not) does not precede a present-tense verb except when it has the sense of the present, nor a past-tense verb except when it is close to the present.

It is said: "I threaded the thread into the needle" (salaktu al-khayta fi al-ibra), and "I caused it to be threaded" (asaltuhu) when I put it into it and strung it. It is also read as naslukuhu (we thread it) with reference to the Reminder (al-dhikr), meaning: like that threading, and similar to it: "We thread the Reminder into the hearts of the guilty," in the sense that He casts it into their hearts [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is that He casts it into their hearts while denying it..." etc. Ahmad said: What is intended, and God knows best, is establishing the proof against the deniers: that God threaded the Qur'an into their hearts and inserted it into their innermost core, just as He threaded it into the hearts of the believers who affirm it. So these people denied it and those people affirmed it, each with knowledge and understanding, "so that whoever perished might perish upon clear evidence, and whoever lived might live upon clear evidence" (Qur'an 8:42). And so that the unbelievers would have no proof against God, claiming that they did not understand the aspects of its inimitability as the believers understood them. So God informed them, now while they are still in a period of respite and capacity, that they did not disbelieve except knowingly, as obstinate, rebellious, and not excusable. And God knows best. For this reason God followed it with His saying: "Even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven and they continued ascending through it, they would surely say: 'Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched'" (Qur'an 15:14–15). That is: these people understood the Qur'an and knew the aspects of its inimitability, and that entered their hearts and settled there; but they are a people whose disposition is obstinacy and whose nature is contentiousness, such that even if they were led along the clearest path and the path most calling them to faith by necessity of direct witnessing—namely, by opening for them a gate in the sky and making them ascend to it so that they enter through it by day—even then... And to this the Qur'an alludes with His saying "they continued" (zallu), because continuing (zulul) occurs only by day; they would say, after this tremendous and manifest clarification: "Our eyes have only been dazzled, and Muhammad has bewitched us, and these are only illusions with no realities beneath them." So He records against them that they have no excuse in denying through lack of hearing, understanding, or reaching the hearts, or comprehension as others among the affirmers comprehended—because all of that is available to them; rather, what afflicts them is only obstinacy, contentiousness, and persistence, nothing else. And God knows best.]] denying it and mocking it, not accepted—just as if you had a need from a miser and he did not grant it to you, and you said:

"Thus I bring it down upon the base-born" — meaning: such a sending down, I sent it down upon them rejected and unfulfilled.

The position of His saying "they do not believe in it" (la yu'minuna bihi) is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: not believing in it. Or it is an explanation of His saying "thus We thread it" (kadhalika naslukuhu). "The way of the former peoples" (sunnat al-awwalin): their practice which God established in destroying them when they denied their messengers and the Reminder revealed to them. It is a warning to the people of Mecca for their denial.

Recited as yaʿrujūna with both ḍamm and kasra. "Sukkirat" means: bewildered, or blocked from sight, from sakar or sukkar. It is also recited sakkarat with the letter sīn lightened (takhfīf) [[Its saying: "and it is recited sukkirat with lightening": perhaps this is from sakar with fatḥa, just as what comes later is from sukkar with ḍamma. (ʿ)]], meaning: blocked, just as a river is blocked from flowing. And it is recited:

sakirat, from sakar, meaning: bewildered, just as a drunkard is bewildered. The meaning is that these polytheists had reached such extremes of obstinacy that, even if a gate of the sky were opened for them, and an ascent made easy for them by which they could climb up into it, and they saw with their own eyes what they saw, they would say: "This is something we imagine; it has no reality. Muhammad has only bewitched us with it." It has also been said:

The mention of "zulul" (daylight) is to make their ascent occur during the day, so that they would be clear-sighted regarding what they see. He said "innamā" to indicate that they firmly assert that this is nothing but a dazzling of the eyes.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verse 16–20:

"Man" (مَنِ) is in the accusative position as an exception (istithna'). And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they used not to be barred from the heavens; but when 'Isa was born, they were prevented from three heavens, and when Muhammad (ﷺ) was born, they were prevented from all the heavens. ﴿A clear flaming fire﴾ (shihabun mubin): manifest to those who see. ﴿Weighed﴾ (mawzun): weighed by the balance of wisdom and measured by the measure that it requires, such that no addition or subtraction is suitable in it; or, it has weight and measure in matters of blessing and benefit. It has been said: what is weighed, such as gold, silver, copper, iron and others, ﴿means of livelihood﴾ (ma'ayish) with a clear ya'. This differs from the shama'il (qualities) and khaba'ith (vile things) and the like, for making the ya' explicit in them is an error; the correct form is the hamza, or else the ya' is pronounced in an intermediate way (bayn bayn).

It has also been read as ma'a'ish, with a hamza, by analogy (al-tashbih). ﴿And for whom you are not providers﴾ (wa man lastum lahu biraziqin) is coordinated with ma'ayish, or with the position of lakum, as if it were said: "And We made for you therein means of livelihood, and We made for you those for whom you are not providers"; or: "And We made for you means of livelihood, and for those for whom you are not providers." "Mentioning the treasuries is a figurative illustration (tamthil, a parable-like image). The meaning is: there is nothing from which the servants benefit except that We are capable of bringing it into being, creating it, and bestowing it. We give it only in a measured amount that We know to be good for them. So the treasuries are struck as an example of His power over everything that is within His power."

Regarding *lawāqiḥ* (fertilizing), there are two opinions. The first is that the wind is *lāqiḥ* when it brings good, namely the production of rain-bearing clouds, just as it is said of the wind that brings no good: *rīḥ ʿaqīm* (a barren wind). The second is that *al-lawāqiḥ* means *al-malāqiḥ* (the impregnating ones), as in the verse: "And one bewildered by what the calamities (*al-ṭawāʾiḥ*) bring down."

[[Let Yazid be wept for by the one weakened by disputes... and by the seeker of gifts whom the calamities cast down.

This is said by Dirar ibn Nahshal, lamenting his brother Yazid ibn Nahshal. It has also been said otherwise.

*Liyabki* is in the passive voice, the *lām* is for command, *Yazid* is the deputy subject, and *ḍāriʿ* is the subject of an omitted verb. The sentence contains an implied question, as if it were said: "Who weeps for him?" It is answered: "The *ḍāriʿ* (the one weakened), who is the one seeking help, and the *mukhtabiṭ* (the one seeking gifts), who is the one who knocks on the doors of those who are asked." *Mā* is a verbal-source particle, and *tuṭīḥ* means "destroys."

Al-Jawharī said: "*Ṭawwaḥathu al-ṭawāyiḥ*" means "the calamities hurled him down." One does not say *al-muṭawwaḥāt*, and it is among the rare forms; the analogical form would be *al-muṭīḥāt* from *aṭāḥa*, or *al-muṭawwaḥāt* from *ṭawwaḥa*.

So the meaning is: the one seeking gifts weeps for him because of the destruction of his wealth by the calamities, and *mā* is connected to *mukhtabiṭ*. It has also been said that it may be connected to the implied verb, as in the phrase "*al-khuṣūma*."

Al-ʿIṣām related from al-ʿĀrif al-Rūmī that *Yazid* is a vocative, the vocative particle is omitted, and *ḍāriʿ* is the deputy subject, because the *ḍāriʿ* and the *mukhtabiṭ* deserve to be wept for more than Yazid, who used to help them. It is also narrated as *Liyabki Yazīdu* with the active voice and *Yazīda* in the accusative, so *ḍāriʿ* is the subject of the mentioned verb. It is meant as *al-maṭāwiḥ*, the plural of *muṭayḥa*. It is also read *wa-arsalnā al-rīḥ* (in the singular), interpreting it as a collective noun.

Al-Salsal: dry clay that rings (yusalsilu) when it is not fired; when it is fired, it becomes pottery (fakhkhar). They said: if you imagine in its sound a prolonged note, it is ṣalīl; if you imagine in it a reverberation, it is ṣalṣala. It was also said: it is a doubling of ṣall, meaning when it has become foul. Al-Hama' (ḥama'): black, altered mud. Al-Masnun: shaped, from "sunnat al-wajh" [[His saying "sunnat al-wajh" — in al-Sihah: sunnat al-wajh means its form (ṣūratuhu). (ʿA.)]]; and it was said: poured, cast, meaning: he poured the form of a human being as statues are cast from molten substances in their moulds. It was also said: foul, from "sannantu al-ḥajar 'alā al-ḥajar" when I rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is sanīn, and it is only foul.

Min ḥama'in (﴿from black mud﴾) is an attribute of ṣalṣāl, meaning: He created him from clay (ṣalṣāl) that came from black mud (ḥama'). Masnūn in the sense of shaped may be an attribute of ṣalṣāl, as if He poured the mud and shaped from it the image of a hollow human figure, which dried until, when struck, it rang. Then He transformed it after that into another substance.

Wal-jann (﴿and the jinn﴾): for the jinn, as Adam for humankind. It was said: he is Iblis. al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read: wal-jaʾn, with a hamza.

Min nāri al-samūm (﴿from the fire of the scorching wind﴾): from the fire of intense heat that penetrates the pores. It was said: this samūm is one part of seventy parts of the scorching fires from which God created the jinn.

And when your Lord said: remember the time of His saying (to the angels), "I have made him [sawwaytuhu]," meaning I balanced his creation, completed it, and prepared it for the breathing of the spirit into it. The meaning of "and I breathed into him of My Spirit" is that I gave him life. There is no actual blowing and no blown-into thing; rather, it is an image (tamthil) for securing that by which he comes to live.

Iblis was excepted from the angels because he was among them, commanded together with them to prostrate. So the name "the angels" was applied to them as a group, and then he was excepted after that general application, like your saying, "I saw them except Hind."

"And he refused" (abā) is a resumed statement (istinaf), answering an implied question: "Why did he not prostrate?" So it was said: he refused that and was arrogant toward it. It was also said: its meaning is "but Iblis refused."

The preposition governing "an" (that) is elided. Its estimated form in "what is with you that you not be among the prostrators" (*mā laka allā takūna ma' al-sājidīn*) means: what purpose do you have in your refusal to prostrate, and what call is there for you to it?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verses 45–48:

"The absolutely God-fearing (al-muttaqi 'ala l-itlaq)": one who guards against what must be guarded against, namely what He has forbidden. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both:

"Guard against disbelief and immoral acts, and for them are sins which the prayers and other things expiate. ﴿Enter it,﴾ with the intention of a saying (ʿala irada l-qawl)."

Al-Hasan recited: "Adkhulu-ha bi-salamin" (﴿Enter it in peace﴾), meaning "safe ones" (salimin), or "greeting" (musallaman ʿalaykum): the angels greet you. Al-ghull (rancor) is the hatred lodged in the heart, from "insinuated into its inner part and penetrated deep" (inghalla fi jawfihi wa taghalghala). That is: if any of them had a rancor against another in the world, Allah removes that from their hearts and purifies their souls. And from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "I hope that I, ʿUthman, Talha and al-Zubayr will be among them." And from al-Harith al-A'war: "I was sitting with him when the son of Talha came, and ʿAli said to him: 'Welcome, O son of my brother! By Allah, I indeed hope that I and your father will be among those of whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts﴾.' Someone said: 'No! Allah is too just to gather you and Talha in one place.' He said: 'Then to whom does this verse belong, may your mother be bereft?'"[[Related by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Uqayli and Ibn Sa'd by way of al-Harith al-A'war, who said: "I was with ʿAli ibn Abi Talib when ʿImran ibn Talha came to him," and he mentioned it, and in it: "al-Harith—meaning the narrator—said: 'Allah is greater and more just than that.'" There is another route, related by al-Hakim by way of Rabi'i ibn Khirash, who said: "I was sitting with ʿAli when the son of Talha came to him, and he greeted him, and he welcomed him. He said: 'You welcome me, O Commander of the Faithful, when I have been called my father's son and my wealth has been taken?' He said: 'As for your wealth, it is set aside in the treasury; go back and take it. As for your father, I hope that I and your father will be among those of whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts﴾, the verse.' A man from Hamdan said, and he mentioned it." Al-Hakim also related it, and al-Tabari, by way of Abu Habiba, client of Talha, who said: "ʿImran ibn Talha entered upon ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him," and he mentioned something similar.]] Some said: its meaning is that Allah purifies their hearts from envying one another for ranks in Paradise, removes from them every rancor, and places in them mutual affection and love. "Ikhwanan" (brothers) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "ʿAla sururin mutaqabilin" (on couches, facing one another) is likewise. From Mujahid: the couches turn with them wherever they turn, so in all their states they are face to face.

Al-Hasan recited: "Adkhulu-ha bi-salamin" (﴿Enter it in peace﴾), meaning "safe ones" (salimin), or "greeting" (musallaman ʿalaykum): the angels greet you. Al-ghull (rancor) is the hatred lodged in the heart, from "insinuated into its inner part and penetrated deep" (inghalla fi jawfihi wa taghalghala). That is: if any of them had a rancor against another in the world, Allah removes that from their hearts and purifies their souls. And from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "I hope that I, ʿUthman, Talha and al-Zubayr will be among them." And from al-Harith al-A'war: "I was sitting with him when the son of Talha came, and ʿAli said to him: 'Welcome, O son of my brother! By Allah, I indeed hope that I and your father will be among those of whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts﴾.' Someone said: 'No! Allah is too just to gather you and Talha in one place.' He said: 'Then to whom does this verse belong, may your mother be bereft?'"[[Related by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Uqayli and Ibn Sa'd by way of al-Harith al-A'war, who said: "I was with ʿAli ibn Abi Talib when ʿImran ibn Talha came to him," and he mentioned it, and in it: "al-Harith—meaning the narrator—said: 'Allah is greater and more just than that.'" There is another route, related by al-Hakim by way of Rabi'i ibn Khirash, who said: "I was sitting with ʿAli when the son of Talha came to him, and he greeted him, and he welcomed him. He said: 'You welcome me, O Commander of the Faithful, when I have been called my father's son and my wealth has been taken?' He said: 'As for your wealth, it is set aside in the treasury; go back and take it. As for your father, I hope that I and your father will be among those of whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts﴾, the verse.' A man from Hamdan said, and he mentioned it." Al-Hakim also related it, and al-Tabari, by way of Abu Habiba, client of Talha, who said: "ʿImran ibn Talha entered upon ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him," and he mentioned something similar.]] Some said: its meaning is that Allah purifies their hearts from envying one another for ranks in Paradise, removes from them every rancor, and places in them mutual affection and love. "Ikhwanan" (brothers) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "ʿAla sururin mutaqabilin" (on couches, facing one another) is likewise. From Mujahid: the couches turn with them wherever they turn, so in all their states they are face to face.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

When he had completed the mention of promise and threat, he followed it with ﴿Inform My servants﴾, as a confirmation of what was mentioned and as a means of establishing it firmly in the souls.

And from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him): ﴿Forgiving to those who repent, and His punishment is for those who do not repent.﴾ And he conjoined ﴿and inform them﴾ to ﴿Inform My servants﴾, so that they might take what Allah sent down as punishment upon the people of Lut as a lesson (ʿibrah), by which they may take heed of Allah's wrath and His retribution against the criminals, and be certain in His sight that His punishment is the painful punishment.

"Peace" (salaman): meaning, we greet you with peace, or you (plural) said "peace."

"Afraid" (wajilun): frightened. Their fear was because they refrained from eating. It was also said: because they entered without permission and at an improper time.

Al-Hasan recited: lā tuwjal, with a ḍammah on the tā', from awjalahu yūjiluhu, meaning he frightened him. It was also read: lā tuʾjal, and lā tuwājal, from wājalahu, in the sense of awjalahu.

It was read nubashširuka with a fatḥah on the nūn and without shaddah. "Indeed, we give you good news" (innā nubashširuka) is a resumptive clause carrying the sense of a reason for the prohibition of fear: they meant that you are like one secure who is given glad tidings, so do not be afraid. That is, "Do you give me glad tidings although old age has touched me, that a child will be born to me?" That is: birth is an amazing matter, customarily considered strange in the case of old age. "With what then do you give me glad tidings" (fa-bima tubashshirun): the interrogative mā, into which the sense of wonder has entered, as if he said: "With what marvel do you give me glad tidings?" Or he meant: you give me glad tidings of something that is not conceivable in custom, so with what thing do you give glad tidings, meaning: you do not really give me glad tidings of anything, because glad tidings of such a thing are glad tidings of nothing. It is permissible that it not be a complement of bashshara, and that it be a question about the manner and way, meaning: by what way do you give me glad tidings of a child, when glad tidings of it have no way in custom. And his saying, "We have given you glad tidings with the truth" (bashsharnāka bil-ḥaqq): the bāʾ may be a complement, meaning: we have given you glad tidings with certainty that admits no doubt; or we have given you glad tidings by a way that is true, which is the word of God and His promise, and that He is able to bring forth a child without two parents, so how much more from an aged old man and a barren wife.

It was read tubashshirūn, with a fatḥah and with a kasrah on the nūn, by omitting the nūn of the plural, the original being tubashshirūnan and tubashshirūnnī, with the plural nūn assimilated into the nūn of the support (ʿimād). [[His saying "watubashshirūn" with a kasrah on the nūn and shaddah: stated by al-Nasafi. (ʿ)]]

It was read: min al-qāniṭīn (from qanaṭa, yaqnaṭu). It was read: wa man yaqnaṭu, with the three vowels on the nūn. He meant: "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those who are astray from the right path" (illā al-mukhṭiʾūn), or "except the disbelievers," like His saying: "None despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people." That is: I did not find this strange out of despair of His mercy, but out of considering it unlikely according to the custom which God has established.

**Question:** Regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except the family of Lut﴾, is the exception connected (*muttasil*) or disconnected (*munqati'*)?

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask whether the first exception is connected... etc." Ahmad said: Making it disconnected (*munqati'*) is preferable and more plausible. This is because excluding them from the pronoun referring back to "people" (*qawm*), which is indefinite (*nakira*), is remote. The function of an exception is to remove what, were it not for the exception, would have been included in the preceding rule, and such inclusion is impossible with an indefinite noun. For this reason you rarely find an indefinite noun excepted from except in a negative context, because then it becomes more general, so that inclusion would be realized were it not for the exception. Hence "I saw people except Zayd" is not good Arabic, while "I did not see anyone except Zayd" is good. And God knows best.]]

**Answer:** It cannot be other than one of two cases. Either it is an exception from *qawm* (people), in which case it is disconnected, because the people are described as criminals, and so the two categories differ. Or it is an exception from the pronoun in *mujrimin* (criminals), in which case it is connected, as if it were said: "To a people who had all committed crimes, except the family of Lut alone," just as in His saying, ﴿We found therein no house except one house of those who submit﴾ (51:36).

**Question:** Does the meaning differ according to the two exceptions?

**Answer:** Yes. In the disconnected reading, the family of Lut are excluded from the scope of the sending (*irsal*), on the basis that the messengers were sent specifically to the criminal people and were not sent to the family of Lut at all.

The sense of their being sent to the criminal people is like the sending of a stone or an arrow to its target, in the sense of punishment and destruction. It is as if it were said: "We destroyed a criminal people, but We saved the family of Lut."

In the connected reading, they are included in the scope of the sending, and the angels were sent to all of them, to destroy these and to save those. Thus the sending is not restricted to the sense of destruction and punishment as in the first case.

**Question:** With what does ﴿We are to save them﴾ (*innā lamunajjūhum*) connect under both readings?

**Answer:** When the exception is disconnected, it functions like the predicate of *lakinna* ("but") in connection with the family of Lut, because the meaning is: "But the family of Lut are to be saved." When it is connected, the clause is a new independent sentence, as if Abraham, peace be upon him, had said to them: "What is the situation of the family of Lut?" and they replied: "We are to save them."

**Question:** With what is ﴿except his wife﴾ (*illā imra'atahu*) connected, and is it an exception from an exception?

**Answer:** It is an exception from the pronoun in the genitive, in His saying ﴿we are to save them﴾, and it has nothing to do with an exception from an exception. This is because an exception from an exception occurs only when the ruling is the same throughout, and it could be said: "We destroyed them, except the family of Lut, except his wife," just as the ruling is the same in the statement of one who divorces: "You are divorced three times, except two, except one," and in the statement of one who acknowledges a debt: "I owe so-and-so ten dirhams, except three, except one dirham." But in the verse the two rulings differ, because ﴿except the family of Lut﴾ is connected to *arsalna* ("We sent") or to *mujrimin* ("criminals"), while ﴿except his wife﴾ is connected to *lamunajjūhum* ("We are to save them"). So how could it be an exception from an exception?

It is recited *lamunajjūhum* with light and with heavy (intensive) pronunciation.

**Question:** Why is the verb of decree (*qaddarnā*) in His saying ﴿We decreed that she would be among those who remain behind﴾ (*qaddarnā innahā lamina al-ghābirīn*) permitted to take a suspended complement, when suspension is a property of verbs of the heart?

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask why it is permitted for the verb of decree in His saying, ﴿We decreed that she would be among those who remain behind﴾, to take a suspended complement, etc." Ahmad said: This too is one of his Mu'tazilite hidden meanings in denying predestination and decree, and in holding that the matter is newly originated (*anaf*). For they do not believe that God wills most of the actions of His servants, whether acts of disobedience, permissible acts, or the like, nor that He decrees them for the servants, in the sense that He wills them while knowing that they will do other than what He wills and intends. For them, "decree" means knowledge, not will. Then he argued that decree means knowledge, by the fact that the verb of decree is suspended from action, and that is a property of the verb of knowledge and its sisters. So look at the depth of his inquiry and the subtlety of his insight in seeking a verse to fabricate and to oppose with it the clear proofs. In his own words there is evidence against him, for "decree" in his view implies the meaning of knowledge, and a verb which implies another meaning retains its original meaning in addition to the incidental meaning, so that it conveys both together. Thus "decree," in conveying the incidental meaning of knowledge, also conveys will in its original and established meaning. And God knows best. Some people have taken His saying, ﴿We decreed that she would be among those who remain behind﴾, to be from God's own speech and not reported from the angels, and this is the apparent meaning. For whoever makes it the speech of the angels needs an interpretation to attribute the decree to themselves, and he treats it as the manner of royal attendants saying "We arranged such-and-such" or "We commanded such-and-such," while they mean the king arranged and commanded. Al-Zamakhshari resorted to this interpretation, though its basis does not require interpretation: if *qaddarnā* is taken to mean "we knew that she would be among those who remain behind," there is nothing strange in the angels knowing this through God informing them of it. Interpretation is needed only for one who takes *qaddarnā* to mean "we willed and decreed" and makes it the speech of the angels. And God knows best.]]

**Answer:** Because the verb of decree includes the meaning of knowledge. For this reason the scholars explained God's decree of the actions of His servants as knowledge.

**Question:** Why did the angels attribute the verb of decree, which belongs to God alone, to themselves, and not say "God decreed"?

**Answer:** Because of the nearness and special relationship they have with God, which no one other than them has. This is like the king's intimates saying "We arranged such-and-such" and "We commanded such-and-such," when the one who arranges and commands is the king and not them. They only thereby display their closeness and show that they are not distinct from him.

It is also recited *qaddarnā* with light pronunciation.

One says *wajaʿa wajaʿan* like *taʿiba taʿaban*. **Al-layt** (with a kasra) is the side of the neck, and **al-akhdaʿ** is a vein in it. These two are specifications transferred from the subject, and this is hyperbole for the abundance of looking back.]]

Or the prohibition against looking back is a metonymy (*kināya*) for continuing the journey and abandoning delay and stopping, because whoever looks back must make at least a brief pause.

﴿Where you are commanded﴾. It has been said that this refers to Egypt (*miṣr*). The verb *wa-imḍū* (and proceed) is transitive to an indefinite adverb of place, because *ḥaythu* is indefinite regarding places, and the pronoun in *tu'marūna* is likewise.

The verb **qaḍaynā** (We decreed) is transitive with *ilā* because it contains the meaning of *awḥaynā* (We revealed), as if it were said: "And We revealed to him, decreed and determined." **That matter** is explained by His words, ﴿that the last of these people is to be cut off﴾. Leaving it vague and then explaining it magnifies and exalts the matter.

Al-Aʿmash read **inna** with a kasra, as a new (resumed) sentence, as if someone had said: "Tell us about that matter," and it was answered: "Indeed the last of these people..." In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: "And We said, indeed the last of these people..."

**Dābir** means the last of them. The meaning is that they will be completely uprooted, to the very last, so that not one of them will remain.

**The people of the city**: the people of Sodom (Sadūm), whose judge was proverbial for injustice, **rejoicing at the angels**.

The People of al-Hijr (Thamud), and al-Hijr was their valley, which lies between Madina and Syria. It is narrated from Jabir: "We passed with the Prophet (ﷺ) [[I have not found it from the hadith of Jabir. "Secure" (amin) means safe, because the houses were solid and strongly built, so they were secure from collapsing and their structures from falling apart, from thieves breaking in, from enemies, and from the calamities of time. Or they were secure from the punishment of Allah, thinking that the mountains would protect them from it. "What they used to earn" refers to the building of sturdy houses, wealth, and numbers.

Except with truth. Except as a creation bound up with truth and wisdom, not in vain or as mere play. Or it means: by the cause of justice and fairness on the Day of Recompense for deeds. ﴿And indeed the Hour is surely coming﴾, and indeed Allah will take vengeance for you therein upon your enemies, and will recompense you and them for your good deeds and their evil deeds, for He did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except for that. ﴿So overlook﴾, that is, turn away from them and bear what you encounter from them with a beautiful turning away, with forbearance and forgiveness. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verse 87:

sab'an (seven). Seven verses, and these are al-Fatiha. Or seven surahs, and these are the long surahs (al-tiwal), and scholars differed about the seventh. It was said: al-Anfal and Bara'a, because they are in the ruling of one surah, and for this reason they are not separated by the basmala verse. It was also said: Surat Yunus. And it was said: they are the surahs beginning with Ha Mim (Al Ha Mim), or seven scrolls, and these are the "sab'" (sevens). Al-mathani (the oft-repeated) comes from tathniya (repetition), meaning repetition, because al-Fatiha is among the things whose recitation is repeated in prayer and elsewhere. Or it comes from al-thana' (praise), because it includes what is praise of God. The word is "mathnāh" or "mathniyya," and "mathniyya" is an adjective of the verse. As for the surahs or the sevens, it is because of the repetition of narratives, admonitions, promise and threat, and other things that occur in them, and because of the praise in them, as though they praise God Most High for His great acts and His beautiful attributes. The "min" (from) in "min al-mathani" is either explanatory (lil-bayan) or partitive (lil-tab'id) if by the seven you mean al-Fatiha or the long surahs, and explanatory if you mean the sevens. It is permissible that all the books of God are "mathani," because they praise Him, and because of the repeated admonitions in them, and the Qur'an is part of them. If you say: how is it valid to conjoin the Mighty Qur'an with "the seven"? Is this not conjoining a thing with itself? I say: if by the seven you mean al-Fatiha or the long surahs, then what remains after them is called by the name Qur'an, because it is a name that applies to a part as it applies to the whole. Do you not see His saying, "by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an" (12:3), meaning Surat Yusuf? And if you mean the sevens, then the meaning is: We have given you what is called the seven oft-repeated and the Mighty Qur'an, i.e., the one combining these two attributes, which are praise or repetition, and greatness.

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 15, verses 88–89:

That is: do not strain your gaze with the longing of one who desires and covets what We have given to pairs of them, categories of disbelievers. If you say: how does this connect with what precedes it? [Mahmud said: "If you say how does this connect with what precedes it..." Ahmad said: This is the correct interpretation of the meaning of the hadith, and many scholars have understood it as referring to singing (al-ghina'). These scholars claimed that "taghanna" is derived only from al-ghina' (singing), with the long vowel, and not from al-ghina' (wealth) with the short vowel, and that its verb form is istaghna specifically. But I have found the form tataghanna from al-ghina' with the short vowel in the sound hadith about horses. As for the one who is "a veil," it is a man who tied it out of tagharrun (self-control) and ta'affuf (chastity). This is definitely and by consensus from al-ghina' with the short vowel, and it is the verbal noun of ta'anna. This shows that it is used in both forms, contrary to the claim of the opponent, and God is the Granter of success.] I say: He says to the Messenger of God ﷺ:

You have been given the great blessing, and every blessing, however great, is paltry and insignificant in comparison to it, namely the Mighty Qur'an. So you should be content with it, and do not extend your eyes toward the enjoyments of this world. From this is the hadith: "He is not of us who does not sing (yatagharra) the Qur'an [al-Bukhari narrated it through Abu Salama from Abu Hurayra, and there is a parallel on the authority of Sa'd and Abu Lubaba in Abu Dawud. The takhrij scholar says: al-Nawawi and before him al-Mundhiri overlooked it, then al-Tibi attributed it to Abu Dawud and did not attribute it to al-Bukhari, and al-Qurtubi erred in attributing it to Muslim rather than al-Bukhari; the author of Jami' al-Usul did not mention it, and al-Hakim attributed it to the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). What is in the Sahihayn is the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who sings the Qur'an aloud (yataghanna bihi yajharu bihi)." Benefit: al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan, in the Book of Testimonies, that al-Hakim informed us from Abu al-Asamm, who heard al-Rabi' say: I heard al-Shafi'i say: "He is not of us who does not sing (yatafghan) the Qur'an." A man said to him: "Does it mean 'yastaghni' (be content with)?" He said: "That is not its meaning; its meaning is that he recites it with sorrow (tahzin)."]] and the hadith of Abu Bakr: "Whoever has been given the Qur'an and sees that someone has been given something of this world better than what he has been given, has belittled something great and magnified something small [I have not found it from Abu Bakr. Ibn 'Adi narrated it in the biography of Hamza al-Nasibi from Zayd ibn Rafi' from Abu 'Ubayda from Ibn Mas'ud, raised to the Prophet: "Whoever learns the Qur'an and thinks that someone is richer than him has belittled something great and magnified something small." The narrators accused Hamza of fabrication. Ishaq and al-Tabari narrated it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar with the wording: "Whoever has been given the Qur'an and sees that someone has been given better than what he has been given has magnified what God has belittled and belittled what God has magnified..."]]

It was also said: seven caravans from Busra and Adhri'at arrived bearing the goods of the Jews of Banu Qurayza and Banu al-Nadir, containing various kinds of cloth, perfume, jewels and all sorts of goods. The Muslims said: "If these possessions were ours, we would strengthen ourselves with them and spend them in the way of God." God, Mighty and Exalted, said to them: "I have given you seven verses which are better than these seven caravans."

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾: that is, do not wish for their wealth, and do not grieve that they did not believe, so that Islam might be strengthened by their position and the believers might be lifted up by them. Be humble toward those with you among the poor and weak believers, and be content regarding the faith of the rich and powerful. ﴿And say: Indeed I am the clear warner﴾: I warn you with clear proof and evidence that God's punishment is descending upon you.

This shows that it is used in both forms, contrary to the claim of the opponent, and God is the Granter of success.] I say: He says to the Messenger of God ﷺ:

You have been given the great blessing, and every blessing, however great, is paltry and insignificant in comparison to it, namely the Mighty Qur'an. So you should be content with it, and do not extend your eyes toward the enjoyments of this world. From this is the hadith: "He is not of us who does not sing (yatagharra) the Qur'an [al-Bukhari narrated it through Abu Salama from Abu Hurayra, and there is a parallel on the authority of Sa'd and Abu Lubaba in Abu Dawud. The takhrij scholar says: al-Nawawi and before him al-Mundhiri overlooked it, then al-Tibi attributed it to Abu Dawud and did not attribute it to al-Bukhari, and al-Qurtubi erred in attributing it to Muslim rather than al-Bukhari; the author of Jami' al-Usul did not mention it, and al-Hakim attributed it to the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). What is in the Sahihayn is the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who sings the Qur'an aloud (yataghanna bihi yajharu bihi)." Benefit: al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan, in the Book of Testimonies, that al-Hakim informed us from Abu al-Asamm, who heard al-Rabi' say: I heard al-Shafi'i say: "He is not of us who does not sing (yatafghan) the Qur'an." A man said to him: "Does it mean 'yastaghni' (be content with)?" He said: "That is not its meaning; its meaning is that he recites it with sorrow (tahzin)."]] and the hadith of Abu Bakr: "Whoever has been given the Qur'an and sees that someone has been given something of this world better than what he has been given, has belittled something great and magnified something small [I have not found it from Abu Bakr. Ibn 'Adi narrated it in the biography of Hamza al-Nasibi from Zayd ibn Rafi' from Abu 'Ubayda from Ibn Mas'ud, raised to the Prophet: "Whoever learns the Qur'an and thinks that someone is richer than him has belittled something great and magnified something small." The narrators accused Hamza of fabrication. Ishaq and al-Tabari narrated it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar with the wording: "Whoever has been given the Qur'an and sees that someone has been given better than what he has been given has magnified what God has belittled and belittled what God has magnified..."]]

It was also said: seven caravans from Busra and Adhri'at arrived bearing the goods of the Jews of Banu Qurayza and Banu al-Nadir, containing various kinds of cloth, perfume, jewels and all sorts of goods. The Muslims said: "If these possessions were ours, we would strengthen ourselves with them and spend them in the way of God." God, Mighty and Exalted, said to them: "I have given you seven verses which are better than these seven caravans."

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾: that is, do not wish for their wealth, and do not grieve that they did not believe, so that Islam might be strengthened by their position and the believers might be lifted up by them. Be humble toward those with you among the poor and weak believers, and be content regarding the faith of the rich and powerful. ﴿And say: Indeed I am the clear warner﴾: I warn you with clear proof and evidence that God's punishment is descending upon you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verses 90–91:

If you ask: with what does His saying ﴿as We sent down﴾ connect? I answer: there are two possibilities. The first is that it connects with His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you [the seven oft-repeated verses and the magnificent Qur'an]﴾, meaning: We sent down to you the like of what We sent down to the People of the Book, and they are the ones who divided [the Scripture], ﴿who have made the Qur'an into parts﴾, when they said, out of their obstinacy and hostility, that part of it is true, agreeing with the Torah and the Gospel, and part of it is false, contrary to both. So they divided it into true and false, and ʿaḍḍū it [[His saying "wa-ʿaḍḍūhu" (and they divided it into parts). In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ʿaḍaytu al-shāt taʿḍiyatan, if I divided the sheep into limbs; and ʿaḍaytu al-shayʾ taʿḍiyatan, if I separated it. (ʿ)]]. It was also said: they used to mock it, one of them saying, "The Surah of the Cow is mine," and another saying, "The Surah of the Family of ʿImrān is mine." It is also permissible that by "the Qur'an" is meant what they recite of their books, which they have divided by their distortion, and that the Jews affirmed part of the Torah and denied part of it, and the Christians affirmed part of the Gospel and denied part of it. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the conduct of his people toward the Qur'an, their denial of it, and their saying that it is sorcery, poetry, and fables, [and it shows] that other unbelievers did with other scriptures the same as what they did. The second possibility is that it connects with His saying: ﴿And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner"﴾, meaning: warn the Quraysh of the like of the punishment We sent down upon the dividers, meaning the Jews, which befell Qurayẓa and al-Naḍīr. He made what is expected equivalent to what has occurred, and this is among the miracles, because it is a report of what will happen and it did happen. It is also permissible that ﴿those who made the Qur'an into parts﴾ be in the accusative by virtue of "the warner," meaning: warn the ones who divide the Qur'an into sorcery, poetry, and fables, [warn them] of the like of what We sent down upon the dividers, who are the twelve who divided the entrances of Mecca during the season of pilgrimage. They sat at each entrance, dispersed, to turn people away from belief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), each saying: "Do not be deceived by the one who comes out from among us, for he is a sorcerer," and another saying, "He is a liar," and another, "He is a poet." Allah destroyed them on the Day of Badr and before it by calamities, such as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib, and others. Or [it means] the like of what We sent down upon the group who swore among themselves to attack Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) by night, and al-iqtisām means the same as al-taqāsum. If you ask: when you connect His saying ﴿as We sent down﴾ with His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you﴾, what is the meaning of the intervening of ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾ to the end [of the verse] between them? I answer: because that [passage] is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding their denial and hostility, it interposed what supplements the meaning of consolation: the prohibition against turning toward their worldly life and grieving over their disbelief, and the command that he turn with his whole being toward the believers.

ʿiḍīn means parts, the plural of ʿiḍah, and its root is ʿiḍwah on the pattern fiʿlah, from ʿaḍā al-shāt, when one makes it into limbs. Ru'ba said:

"And the religion of Allah is not one to be divided."

It was also said: it is fiʿlah from ʿaḍahtuhu, when I slandered him [[His saying "idhā bahtahu" means: I accused him. (ʿ)]]. It is reported from ʿIkrima that al-ʿiḍah means sorcery, in the dialect of the Quraysh, who call a female sorceress ʿāḍihah. The Prophet (ﷺ) cursed the ʿāḍihah [[Recorded by Abū Yaʿlā and Ibn ʿAdī from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās. In its chain is Zamʿah ibn Ṣāliḥ, from Salama ibn Wahram, and both are weak. It has a witness in ʿAbd al-Razzāq through a narration from Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ.]] and the mustaʿḍihah. Its letter that is dropped is a waw according to the first view, and a hāʾ according to the second.

"We will surely question them" is an expression for a threat (wa'id, a warning of punishment). It was also said: He asks them a question of rebuke (taqri', reproach). And from Abu al-'Aliyah: The servants will be asked about two things: what they used to worship, and what they answered the messengers.

**Surah 15, verse 94:** "So proclaim openly what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists."

Fa-iṣda' bimā tu'mar: fa-jhar bihi wa-azhirh (openly declare it and make it manifest). It is said: ṣada'a bil-ḥujjah (he expounded the proof) when he spoke it aloud, like your saying ṣarraḥa bihā (he made it clear). It derives from al-ṣadīʿ, which is the dawn, and al-ṣad' in glass means clarity of separation. It is also said:

fa-iṣda' fa-farroq bayna al-ḥaqq wa'l-bāṭil bimā tu'mar (so separate and distinguish between truth and falsehood with what you are commanded), and the meaning is: with what you are commanded of the sacred laws (sharāʾiʿ), so the preposition has been omitted, as in the verse of the poet:

*amartuka al-khayra fa-if'al mā umirta bih*
*fa-qad taraktuka dhā māl wa-dhā nashab*

(Commentary on the verse, as in the text: "He said to me the word of one of sound judgment and strength...")

[Translation of the cited poem and its commentary follows, as in the source:]

*Fa-qāla lī qawlu dhī ra'yin wa-maqdarah... muḥarrar nazih khāl min al-rayb*
*amartuka al-khayra fa-if'al mā umirta bih... fa-qad taraktuka dhā māl wa-dhā nashab*

It is attributed to Khifaf ibn Nadbah, and it is said to Abbas ibn Mirdas, and it is said to Amr ibn Ma'dikarib, and it is said to Lā'ās ibn Mūsā. Al-maqdarah (power) has its dāl vowelled three ways, meaning strength. Al-muḥarrar al-nazih (pure, unblemished, like ḥadhar) means free of adulteration. Al-rayb means doubt, and it is an attribute (naʿt) of dhū ra'y.

If you made it an attribute of al-ra'y, there would be a separation between the attribute and the thing described by the conjunction. It is permissible to put it in the nominative as a detached attribute of the saying.

Al-nashab: wealth, original, silent or speaking; it is thus a general term after a specific one. It is narrated as dhā nasab, with the unpointed letter (sīn), meaning great lineage. Amara is transitive to the second object with bi-. It is said: amartuka al-khayra by extension (tawassuʿ), or by implicit meaning of imposing an obligation (tadmīn al-taklīf), and the poet combined both in the verse.

It is also permissible for bimā to be a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), meaning "by your command," as a verbal noun from the passive form.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 15, verses 95–96:

On the authority of ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr regarding the mockers: they were five men, men of rank and standing: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and al-Harith ibn al-Talatila.

And on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him): they all died before Badr. Jibril (peace be upon him) said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to suffice you against them." So he pointed to the shin of al-Walid, and an arrow passed by and became lodged in his garment. He did not bend down out of pride, so it struck a vein in his heel and severed it, and he died. He pointed to the sole of the foot of al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, and a thorn entered it. He said, "I have been stung, I have been stung," and his leg swelled until it became like a millstone, and he died. He pointed to the eyes of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he went blind. He pointed to the nose of al-Harith ibn Qays, and he discharged pus through his nose and died. And (he pointed) to al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth while he was sitting at the base of a tree, so he began striking his head against the tree and his face with thorns until he died. [[I have not found it in this wording. It was narrated by al-Tabarani in his two Mu'jams, and by Abu Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqi in their Dala'il, and by Ibn Mardawayh, all through the chain of Jaʿfar ibn Iyas, from Saʿid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding Allah's words: ﴿Indeed We suffice you against the mockers﴾. He said: They are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Abu Zamʿa, and al-Harith ibn Ayṭal al-Sahmi. He said: Jibril came to him and complained of them to him, and he showed him al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, so Jibril pointed to his vein (akhal). He said: "What have you done?" He said: "I have sufficed him." Then he related the hadith. He said: As for al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, he passed by a man from Khuzaʿa who was feathering an arrow of his, and it struck his vein and severed it. As for al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, he went blind. As for al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, sores broke out on his head and he died of them. As for al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, he rode to al-Taʾif, and his donkey was tied to a shibraqa, meaning a thorn; it entered the sole of his foot and killed him. As for al-Harith ibn Ayṭal, the pain of al-asfar (a bilious ailment) seized his stomach until his excrement came out of his mouth, and he died of it.]].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 15, verses 97–99:

﴿بِما يَقُولُونَ﴾ means "at what they say," that is, the slanders of those who attack you and the Qur'an. ﴿فَسَبِّحْ﴾ means: so turn to God for refuge in whatever afflicts you. Turning to God for refuge is constant remembrance and abundant prostration. It will suffice you and remove your distress. ﴿وَدُمْ عَلَى عِبادَةِ رَبِّكَ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَكَ الْيَقِينُ﴾: "yaqin" here means death. That is, as long as you are alive, do not neglect worship.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer. [[Discussed earlier in al-Baqarah.]]

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Hijr will have ten good deeds recorded for him, equal to the number of the Emigrants (muhajirun), the Helpers (ansar), and those who mocked Muhammad (ﷺ)." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi through the route of Abu al-Khalil, from Ali ibn Zayd, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Its chains were discussed earlier at the end of Al 'Imran.]]
